quote: Beweise zu dem Zweck, dass wenn auf einer Fläche $f=0$ eine Curve $N^{te}$ Ordnung gegeben ist, stets eine [-C-] Curve von einer kleineren Ordnung als $N$ gefunden werden kann, so dass diese mit der früheren Curve den vollen [-Sy-] Schnitt von $f=0$ mit einer anderen Fläche bildet —— vorausgesetzt, dass $N > \#$ ist als eine nur von der Fläche $f=0$ abhängigen Grenze
english: For this purpose prove that if a curve of order N is given on a surface f=0, a curve of order smaller than N can always be found such that together with the earlier curve it forms the full intersection of f=0 with another surface — provided that N exceeds a bound depending only on the surface f=0
topic: Notes on the theory of fields as a theory of the four arithmetic operations (Körper, Feld, Ring, Gitter), a claim that the only one-to-one, continuous, differentiable map of the rationals between 0 and 1 onto themselves is a linear fractional function, and the finiteness of the number of ideal classes for a field of algebraic functions of two variables.

triage.modern_statement: Let S = {f=0} ⊂ P^3 be a fixed algebraic surface. Hilbert's claim is that there is a bound B(S), depending only on S, with this property: whenever C ⊂ S is a curve of degree N > B(S), there is a surface G (not containing S) whose intersection with S is C ∪ C', where C' is a curve of degree less than N. In modern language, every curve of large enough degree on S is directly linked (in the sense of liaison theory), by a complete intersection S ∩ G, to a curve of smaller degree on the same surface. Equivalently, for some m, the divisor class mH − C on S is effective and has degree less than N, where H is the hyperplane class. The page says he wanted this to prove that a field of algebraic functions of two variables has finitely many ideal classes, i.e. that divisors on S are bounded modulo complete intersections.
triage.answered_by: I found no source that states or proves this exact lemma. Two related bodies of work exist. (1) Liaison (linkage) of space curves through complete intersections, which goes back to Halphen and Noether (1882–83) and was developed later by Gaeta, Peskine–Szpiro and others. (2) Hilbert's end goal of finitely many divisor classes does not hold as stated for surfaces, because the Picard group can have a continuous part. The correct finiteness result is the Theorem of the Base (Severi; Néron), which says the Néron–Severi group (divisors modulo algebraic equivalence) is finitely generated.

evidence.claim: Linkage, also called liaison, has been used heavily to classify curves in P3 since the work of Halphen and Noether (1883). A curve C is 'directly linked' to the residual curve L in a complete intersection X = C ∪ L.
Liaison began in the nineteenth century as a tool for studying space curves (Noether and others). Gaeta's work was seminal for liaison theory, which is described as an active area.
Szpiro's 1975–76 lectures (with Ferrand, Gruson and Peskine) took up Halphen's work on the equations defining space curves, including liaison.
The Theorem of the Base: the Néron–Severi group of a proper variety (line bundles modulo algebraic equivalence) is finitely generated.
Néron and Severi proved that the Néron–Severi group NS(X) is finitely generated.

triage.why: The problem is clearly a research-level statement about linkage of curves on a fixed surface. It was meant as a lemma toward finiteness of divisor (ideal) classes on algebraic surfaces. My searches turned up the general framework, liaison theory and the Theorem of the Base, but no source that states or settles Hilbert's exact bounded-degree linkage claim. So I cannot cite a resolution. Liaison theory is still being researched, but whether anyone works on this specific statement is unclear. One observation of my own, not taken from any source: the claim cannot hold for reducible curves. On a smooth quadric surface, a curve of type (0,b) (b disjoint lines of one ruling) only has residual classes (m, m−b) with m ≥ b, whose degree 2m−b is at least b. So Hilbert must have meant irreducible curves or some other restriction. His overall goal of finitely many ideal classes also fails as stated in general. What is true is the weaker finiteness modulo algebraic equivalence (Severi; Néron). It is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem.
